questions.question: In PLONK’s generic gate, what are the selector values (qL, qR, qM, qO, qC) conceptually?
options: Per-row coefficients that choose which arithmetic relation a row enforces
A prover-chosen random mask that hides witness values
A hash of the witness columns used to derive Fiat–Shamir challenges
A permutation of rows that enforces copy constraints
questions.explanation: Selectors are fixed coefficients (often preprocessed polynomials) that define the gate equation row-by-row.

questions.question: What is a copy constraint in a circuit arithmetization?
options: An equality requirement between two (or more) witness cells that represent the same variable
A requirement that the prover sends two identical copies of the proof for redundancy
A constraint that forces every row to be a multiplication gate
A rule that the verifier must re-compute the witness from public inputs
questions.explanation: Copy constraints say that values appearing in different places in the witness table must be equal because they are the same logical variable.

questions.question: Which equation is the standard PLONK generic gate constraint at a row i?
options: qL[i]·a[i] + qR[i]·b[i] + qM[i]·a[i]·b[i] + qO[i]·c[i] + qC[i] = 0
a[i] + b[i] + c[i] = 0 (always)
qL[i]·a[i] + qR[i]·b[i] = qM[i]·c[i]
questions.explanation: The generic gate uses five selectors to express addition, multiplication, constants, and combinations in a single per-row identity.

questions.question: Why are the random challenges β and γ introduced in the permutation (copy-constraint) argument?
options: To make it overwhelmingly unlikely that an incorrect wiring passes the product check by coincidence
To guarantee that the witness values are uniformly random
To remove the need for any boundary condition on the grand product Z
To allow the verifier to skip checking gate constraints
questions.explanation: β and γ randomize the products so that equality of products implies the intended permutation property except with negligible probability.

questions.question: What boundary condition is typically enforced for the grand product Z in a permutation argument?
options: Z starts at 1 and ends at 1 over the domain
Z starts at 0 and ends at 0 over the domain
Z must be equal to the witness column a everywhere
Z must be a constant polynomial chosen by the verifier
questions.explanation: The recurrence defines Z as a running product; forcing it to start and end at 1 is what pins down the permutation check.

questions.question: In this lesson’s toy implementation, what is the biggest reason it is not a real SNARK proof system yet?
options: It has no polynomial commitments/opening proofs, so the verifier effectively sees the full witness table
It uses SHA-256 instead of a SNARK-friendly hash like Poseidon
It uses Python instead of Rust, so it cannot be secure
It only supports addition gates and cannot express multiplication
questions.explanation: PLONK needs commitments plus succinct opening proofs to make verification small without revealing the witness.

questions.question: Attack scenario: what can go wrong if the prover can choose β,γ without hashing the full transcript (e.g., missing some absorbed messages)?
options: The proof can become malleable or unsound because challenges are no longer bound to the exact commitments being verified
The proof becomes information-theoretically secure in the standard model
The verifier gains the secret witness from the transcript
The gate constraint identity becomes unnecessary
questions.explanation: Fiat–Shamir challenges must be derived from the exact transcript; missing absorbs can let an attacker adapt messages to the challenges.

questions.question: Why do production PLONKish implementations usually require the domain size n to be a power of two?
options: To use FFT/NTT algorithms for fast polynomial operations over the evaluation domain
Because finite fields only exist for power-of-two sizes
Because permutation arguments only work when n is a power of two
Because Fiat–Shamir hashing requires power-of-two transcript lengths
questions.explanation: Power-of-two domains enable efficient FFT-based interpolation/evaluation, which dominates prover performance.
